findings.issue: Source: "Thus heedfully did Priam and his servant see to the yolking of their cars"; candidate says they "finished yoking their carriages", adding that the work was being completed ("finished") and rendering cars as carriages.
findings.fix: Priam and his servant carefully saw to the yoking of their vehicles at the palace. Then Hecuba came up to them, heavy with sorrow, carrying a golden goblet of wine in her right hand so that they could pour a drink-offering before leaving. She stopped in front of the horses and said, “Take this and pour a drink-offering to father Zeus. You are determined to go to the ships against my wishes, so pray that you return safely from the hands of your enemies. Pray to the son of Cronus, lord of the whirlwind, who sits on Ida and looks down over all Troy. Ask him to send his swift messenger to your right, the bird of omen that is strongest and dearest to him of all birds, so that you see it with your own eyes and can trust it as you set out for the ships of the Danaans. If all-seeing Zeus will not send you this messenger, then however set on going you may be, I would not have you approach the ships of the Argives.”

findings.issue: Source "if so be he may have mercy upon me" is rendered "in case he may have mercy on me", which reads as a precaution and is ungrammatical-sounding; the sense is hope.
findings.fix: Priam answered, “Wife, I will do as you ask. It is good to lift hands in prayer to Zeus, in the hope that he may have mercy on me.”

findings.issue: Source "the flying night" / "darkness of the flying night" is rendered "the rushing night" here but "the fleeting night" in p44; the same Butler phrase should have one rendering.
findings.fix: When the old man heard this, his heart failed him and he was in great fear. He stayed where he was as if dazed, and the hair stood on end all over his body. But the bringer of good luck came up, took him by the hand, and said, “Where, father, are you driving your mules and horses like this, in the dead of night, when other men are asleep? Are you not afraid of the fierce Achaeans, so cruel and relentless, who are close by? If one of them saw you carrying so much treasure through the darkness of the fleeting night, what would become of you? You are no longer young, and the man with you is too old to protect you from those who would attack you. As for me, I will do you no harm, and I will defend you against anyone else, for you remind me of my own father.”

findings.issue: Source: "I have steeled myself as no man yet has ever steeled himself before me"; candidate says only "I have done what no man on earth has done before me", dropping the self-steeling.
findings.fix: When a cruel blow of fate has made a man kill someone in his own country, and he has to flee to a great man’s protection in a land of strangers, everyone who sees him is amazed. Achilles was amazed in just that way when he saw Priam. The others looked at one another in amazement too. Then Priam begged Achilles, saying, “Think of your father, Achilles, you who are like the gods. He is as old as I am, standing on the sad threshold of old age. Perhaps his neighbors are harassing him, and there is no one to keep war and ruin away from him. Yet when he hears that you are still alive, he is glad, and every day he hopes to see his dear son come home to him from Troy. But I am a wretched man. I had the bravest sons in all Troy, and not one of them is left. I had fifty sons when the Achaeans came here. Nineteen of them came from a single womb, and the others were borne to me by the women of my household. Fierce Ares has laid most of them low. Hector was the only one left, the guardian of our city and of ourselves, and you killed him not long ago. That is why I have now come to the ships of the Achaeans, to ransom his body from you with a great ransom. Fear the anger of heaven, Achilles. Think of your own father and pity me. I am more pitiable than he, because I have steeled myself as no man on earth has ever done before me. I have raised to my lips the hand of the man who killed my son.”

findings.issue: Source: "he first took it to a place where Priam should not see it" (Achilles himself carries it); candidate says "First he had it taken to a place", making servants the agent.
findings.fix: The old man was afraid of him and obeyed. Then the son of Peleus sprang out through the door of his house like a lion. He did not go alone. His two squires, Automedon and Alcimus, went with him. Now that Patroclus was dead, he valued these two above all his other comrades. They unyoked the horses and mules, and told Priam’s herald and attendant to sit inside the house. They lifted the ransom for Hector’s body down from the wagon, but left two mantles and a fine shirt for Achilles to wrap the body in when it was given back to be taken home. Then Achilles called to his servants and told them to wash the body and anoint it. First he took it himself to a place where Priam could not see it. He was afraid that Priam, seeing it, might break out in the bitterness of his grief and enrage him, so that he would kill the old man and sin against the word of Zeus. When the servants had washed and anointed the body and wrapped it in a fair shirt and mantle, Achilles himself lifted it onto a bier, and he and his men laid it on the wagon. As he did so he cried aloud and called on his dear comrade by name. “Do not be angry with me, Patroclus,” he said, “if you learn, even in the house of Hades, that I gave Hector back to his father for a ransom. It was not an unworthy one, and I will share it with you fairly.”

findings.issue: Source: "he laid his hand on the old man's right wrist"; candidate "took the old man by the right wrist" turns a reassuring touch into a grasp.
findings.fix: As he spoke he laid his hand on the old man’s right wrist, as a sign that he should have no fear. So Priam and his attendant slept there in the forecourt, their minds full of thought. Achilles lay in an inner room of the house, with fair Briseis beside him.

findings.issue: Source "Jove ... bids you come to him" / "so bid me" is softened to "calls you" / "call me"; also "lead at the end of an ox-horn" gains the word "line". Both are acceptable clarifications.
